fatwas.title: Combining Prayers While Traveling
fatwas.question: I frequently travel for work and it is difficult to pray each salah at its designated time while on the road. Am I permitted to combine Zuhr with Asr, and Maghrib with Isha, during travel?
fatwas.answer:
In the Ḥanafī madhhab, combining two obligatory prayers by performing them both within the time of one (jam' haqīqī) is not permitted, whether one is traveling or resident, except on the Day of 'Arafah and in Muzdalifah during Ḥajj. This is the well-established position of the majority of the Ḥanafī jurists, based on the narrations describing the Prophet ﷺ praying each salah within its own appointed time even during his journeys.

However, the Ḥanafī madhhab does permit what is termed jam' ṣūrī (a 'formal' combination), where one delays Zuhr to the very end of its time and then, immediately after, prays Asr at the very beginning of its time. Outwardly this resembles combining, but in reality each prayer is still performed within its own designated time. This can offer real relief to a traveler without compromising the integrity of the prescribed prayer times.

We would also remind the traveling questioner of the concession of qaṣr (shortening the four-rak'ah prayers to two) once the journey reaches the legal distance, which itself substantially eases the burden of prayer while traveling.
fatwas.references: Al-Hidayah, Kitab al-Salah; Radd al-Muhtar (Ibn Abidin), Bab Salat al-Musafir

fatwas.title: Is Zakāt Due on Retirement Accounts (401k/IRA)?
fatwas.question: I have money invested in an employer-sponsored 401(k) retirement account that I cannot access without penalty until I reach retirement age. Is zakāt due on this money every year, or only when I am able to withdraw it?
fatwas.answer:
Zakātable wealth is generally divided into wealth over which one has full ownership and free access (māl mustaqirr), and wealth to which one's access is restricted. Funds locked in a retirement account that cannot be withdrawn without significant penalty fall into a category jurists describe as 'weak ownership' (milk nāqiṣ), since the owner does not have full, unrestricted disposal over the wealth during the restricted period.

Given this, the position we advise is that zakāt does not become obligatory annually on the portion of the retirement account that remains inaccessible. Rather, once you gain access to the funds — for example, upon retirement, resignation, or an early withdrawal — you should calculate one year's zakāt (2.5%) on the full amount received, treating it as wealth that has newly come into your effective possession, and continue paying zakāt annually thereafter as it remains in your possession.

If your plan allows partial withdrawals at any time (even with a penalty), some scholars take the more precautionary view that zakāt should be calculated annually on the net accessible value after the penalty. Given the difference of opinion, a Muslim who wishes to take the more cautious route out of extra piety is free to do so, though it is not obligatory.
fatwas.references: Radd al-Muhtar (Ibn Abidin), Kitab al-Zakat; Fatawa Usmani, vol. 2

fatwas.title: Ruling on Fasting for a Diabetic Who Takes Insulin
fatwas.arabic_title: حكم صيام مريض السكري الذي يستخدم الأنسولين
fatwas.question: My father was recently diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and takes insulin injections twice daily. His doctor has warned that fasting could be dangerous for his health. Is he excused from fasting in Ramadan, and if so, what is required of him?
fatwas.answer:
The general principle in the Sharī'ah is that fasting becomes non-obligatory, and in fact impermissible to the point of harm, upon a person for whom a trustworthy, knowledgeable physician determines that fasting poses a genuine risk to life or a serious risk of worsening an illness. Allah says, 'And do not kill yourselves,' and the concession for the sick to break the fast is explicitly mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah.

If your father's condition is such that his insulin regimen and blood sugar management genuinely cannot accommodate the fast — as determined by his physician, not merely as a precaution — then he is permitted, indeed required, to break his fast on those days. If his condition is expected to improve (for example, through better medication management), he should make up (qaḍā') the missed days once he is able. If his physician determines the condition is chronic and unlikely to improve such that he will never realistically be able to fast, then he falls under the ruling of a person permanently unable to fast, and he is instead obligated to pay fidyah (a compensatory payment, typically calculated as feeding one poor person for each day missed) in place of qaḍā'.

We advise your father to consult his physician about his specific case and to reach out to us directly if his circumstances are more complex than described here, so that a more tailored ruling can be given.
fatwas.references: Al-Hidayah, Kitab al-Sawm; Fatawa Hindiyyah, Kitab al-Sawm

fatwas.title: Conditions for Wiping Over Socks (Masḥ 'alal-Khuffayn) Instead of Washing the Feet
fatwas.question: Is it permissible to wipe over regular cotton socks during wuḍū instead of removing them and washing my feet, especially in winter when it's inconvenient to take them off?
fatwas.answer:
The concession of wiping over the feet-covering (masḥ) in place of washing the feet was originally established for leather khuffayn (leather socks/boots) that are thick enough to stay on the foot without being tied and can be walked in for some distance without tearing. Regular thin cotton or nylon socks do not meet these conditions in the Ḥanafī madhhab, and therefore wiping over them alone is generally not considered sufficient — you would still need to remove them and wash the feet, or wear thick, leather-like khuffayn that meet the conditions.

That said, many contemporary Ḥanafī scholars have noted that if cotton or wool socks are thick enough that water does not seep through them, and they can be walked in for the legally recognized distance without tearing, some jurists extend the concession to them as well, particularly if reinforced with a layer of rubber or leather sole. Given the difference of opinion, we would encourage using purpose-made leather or thickly reinforced khuffayn if you wish to rely on masḥ regularly, to remove any doubt about validity.

The duration of the concession, once conditions are met, is one day and one night (24 hours) for a resident, and three days and three nights for a traveler, beginning from the first wiping after breaking wuḍū while wearing the socks.
fatwas.references: Al-Hidayah, Kitab al-Taharah; Maraqi al-Falah, Bab al-Mash 'alal Khuffayn

fatwas.title: Is It Necessary to Hire a Guide (Muṭawwif) for Ḥajj?
fatwas.arabic_title: حكم الاستعانة بمرشد أو مطوف في الحج
fatwas.question: My family and I are planning to perform Ḥajj this year through a private group without an organized package. Is it obligatory to hire a guide familiar with the rituals, or can we rely on books and videos to learn the rituals ourselves?
fatwas.answer:
Hiring a guide (muṭawwif) is not, strictly speaking, a legal obligation (wājib) for the validity of Ḥajj itself — Ḥajj remains valid so long as its pillars, obligations, and conditions are fulfilled correctly, regardless of who assists you. However, given the complexity of the rituals, the large crowds, the limited windows of time for certain acts (such as the stoning at Minā or standing at 'Arafah), and the ease with which sincere pilgrims can make errors that affect the completeness of their Ḥajj, we strongly recommend that anyone without prior first-hand experience of the rituals travel with, or at minimum consult closely with, someone knowledgeable — whether a formal muṭawwif, an experienced scholar in your group, or a well-vetted Ḥajj guide service.

Learning from books and videos beforehand is praiseworthy and necessary preparation, but it is not a full substitute for real-time guidance once you are amid the actual rites, where conditions on the ground (crowd flow, timing, physical positioning) often differ from what is described in texts. Many of the errors we are asked about after Ḥajj season stem precisely from pilgrims who studied the rituals well in principle but had no one to consult when an unexpected situation arose in the moment.

If you do travel independently, we would advise identifying, before departure, at least one qualified 'ālim or experienced hajji reachable by phone throughout your trip for any rulings that arise.
fatwas.references: Al-Hidayah, Kitab al-Manasik; Lubab fi Sharh al-Kitab, Kitab al-Hajj

fatwas.title: Can a Wife Stipulate Conditions in the Marriage Contract (Nikāḥ)?
fatwas.question: Before my daughter's nikāḥ, she wishes to include a condition in the contract that she may pursue graduate studies after marriage and that her husband will not prevent her from doing so. Is it valid to include such a condition in the marriage contract, and is her husband bound by it?
fatwas.answer:
It is permissible, and indeed encouraged as good practice, for a wife (or her guardian on her behalf) to stipulate reasonable conditions in the marriage contract that serve her legitimate interests, so long as those conditions do not contradict the essential purposes of marriage or make lawful what Allah has made unlawful (or vice versa). A condition such as permission to pursue education, to continue working in a permissible field, or to live in a particular city, falls within the category of valid conditions according to a significant number of Ḥanafī jurists who follow the position that such conditions, while not strictly binding in the sense of voiding the marriage if broken, do create a moral and, in many contemporary fatwa councils' view, a binding contractual obligation upon the husband.

The classical Ḥanafī position historically held that conditions not intrinsic to the essence of the marriage contract (such as this one) do not have independent binding force — the marriage remains valid, and the mahr and other essentials are unaffected, but the condition itself was traditionally seen as more of a moral undertaking than a legally enforceable term. However, many contemporary Ḥanafī muftis, drawing on the strong precedent of 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him) enforcing such stipulations, and recognizing the compelling need (ḥāja) of the age, hold that such conditions should be treated as binding upon the husband, and that a wife may seek judicial khul' or annulment through a qualified Islamic court or council if he violates it without valid excuse.

We would strongly encourage that this condition be written clearly and explicitly into the marriage contract itself (not left as a verbal understanding), so both families and the officiant are aware of it, and so it may be referred to and, if needed, enforced later.
fatwas.references: Radd al-Muhtar (Ibn Abidin), Kitab al-Nikah; Al-Fatawa al-Hindiyyah, Kitab al-Nikah

fatwas.title: Ruling on Taking an Interest-Free Loan from a Family Member to Start a Business
fatwas.arabic_title: حكم أخذ قرض حسن من أحد الأقارب لبدء مشروع تجاري
fatwas.question: My uncle has offered to lend me $20,000, interest-free, to help start a small business, on the condition that I repay it in monthly installments over three years. Is this arrangement permissible, and are there any conditions I should be aware of to keep it fully halal?
fatwas.answer:
An interest-free loan (qarḍ ḥasan) of this kind is not only permissible but is praised in the Sharī'ah as an act of great virtue; the Prophet ﷺ described lending as being even more meritorious than charity in some respects, since it preserves the dignity of the recipient while still providing real assistance. There is no impermissibility whatsoever in your uncle lending you $20,000 to be repaid over time in fixed monthly installments, so long as the amount to be repaid remains exactly equal to the amount borrowed — no more and no less.

The key condition to safeguard is that the repayment schedule (three years, in this case) must not be tied to any additional amount charged for the extension of time. A loan where repayment is deferred over time in exchange for paying back more than what was borrowed constitutes ribā (usury) and is strictly prohibited, regardless of how it is labeled or how small the excess amount is. As long as you and your uncle agree that exactly $20,000 will be repaid in total, spread across however many installments you agree upon, the arrangement is entirely sound.

We would also advise documenting the loan agreement in writing, specifying the amount, the repayment schedule, and both parties' names, in line with the Qur'anic instruction in Sūrah al-Baqarah to record debts — this protects both you and your uncle from future disputes or misunderstandings, even though it is a family arrangement built on trust.
fatwas.references: Al-Hidayah, Kitab al-Buyu'; Fiqh al-Mu'amalat, Bab al-Qard

fatwas.title: Ruling on Consuming Products Containing Gelatin of Unknown Source
fatwas.arabic_title: حكم تناول المنتجات المحتوية على الجيلاتين مجهول المصدر
fatwas.question: Many candies, marshmallows, and desserts sold in regular grocery stores list 'gelatin' as an ingredient without specifying whether it is derived from beef, pork, or fish. Is it permissible to consume these products when the source of the gelatin is not disclosed?
fatwas.answer:
Gelatin is a protein derived through the processing of animal collagen, most commonly sourced from the skin, bones, and connective tissue of cattle, pigs, or fish. Its ruling in Islamic law depends entirely on its source: gelatin derived from properly slaughtered (dhabīḥa) cattle or other zabīḥa-eligible animals is permissible, gelatin derived from fish is generally permissible according to the majority view, but gelatin derived from swine is unequivocally impermissible to consume, as pork and its derivatives are explicitly prohibited in the Qur'an.

Regarding gelatin whose source is genuinely unknown or undisclosed on the packaging, our position, in line with the majority of contemporary fiqh councils, is one of caution rather than blanket permissibility or blanket prohibition. In non-Muslim-majority countries such as the United States, a significant portion of commercially available gelatin is in fact porcine in origin due to the low cost and high availability of pork by-products, which shifts the balance of probability (ghalabat al-ẓann) toward caution for the discerning Muslim consumer.

Given this, we advise avoiding products with unspecified 'gelatin' listed as an ingredient unless the source is confirmed — either through halal certification, direct manufacturer confirmation, or an ingredient label specifying 'beef gelatin,' 'fish gelatin,' or an explicit halal-certified bovine source. Many mainstream brands now offer halal-certified or beef-gelatin alternatives; we would recommend seeking these out rather than the ambiguous, uncertified originals.
fatwas.references: Fiqh al-Sunnah, Kitab al-At'ima; Contemporary Fatawa on Food Ingredients, Islamic Fiqh Academy

fatwas.title: General Ruling on Photography: Is It Permissible in Islam?
fatwas.arabic_title: الحكم العام للتصوير الفوتوغرافي في الإسلام
fatwas.question: There seems to be a lot of disagreement among scholars about whether photography is permissible. Some say all image-making is prohibited based on hadith about picture-makers, while others say photography is different from drawing or painting. What is the correct position on this?
fatwas.answer:
This is indeed a question on which contemporary scholars have differed, and it is important to understand why. The prohibitive hadiths regarding taṣwīr (image-making) were understood by classical jurists to refer primarily to three-dimensional statues and hand-drawn or hand-painted images of animate beings, particularly those associated with idol worship or veneration, given the historical context of the Arabian Peninsula's transition away from idolatry. The concern centered on the act of 'creating' a form resembling a living being, seen as an imitation of Allah's unique creative power, and on the potential for such images to be venerated.

A significant number of contemporary Ḥanafī scholars, including several respected muftis of the past century, have distinguished mechanical photography (using a camera to capture an already-existing reality via light and chemical or digital processes) from hand-drawn taṣwīr, reasoning that the photographer is not 'creating a form' in the sense the hadiths describe, but merely capturing an image of something that already exists — much like a mirror reflection. On this basis, general photography for identification documents, education, journalism, family memories, and other permissible purposes has been deemed permissible by many contemporary fatwa bodies.

That said, other respected scholars maintain the more cautious traditional position that the prohibition applies broadly to any image of an animate being, photographic or otherwise, and view the permissive contemporary rulings as a concession to necessity (ḍarūra) rather than an unqualified original permissibility. Given this valid difference of opinion, we would advise avoiding unnecessary photography of people out of caution, while recognizing that those who rely on the permissive view have a sound basis to do so, particularly where a genuine need exists (identification, education, official documentation, and the like). In all cases, images should never be used for immodest, idolatrous, or otherwise sinful purposes.
fatwas.references: Fatawa Mahmudiyyah, Kitab al-Adab; Contemporary Fiqh Discussions on Taswir
